The array mbira is a modern hand-made instrument, developed by Bill Wesley from the 1960s and made with Patrick Hadley in San Diego, California. It belongs to the lamellophone family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 122. High-carbon spring-steel tines are grouped by octave and set staggered on the soundboard, held by screwed crossbars; the player presses the tines down with fingers curled as in a fist and releases them, and the bass is flicked upwards with the pad of the thumb. Hollow and solid bodies both carry dual piezo pickups, which can be split into left and right channels. Musicians such as Sting use it, and it also appears in television and film scores.
陣列姆比拉琴的聆聽場合包括多位音樂家的演奏，例如 Sting、Ry Cooder: Places to hear the array mbira include performances by a number of musicians, among them Sting, Ry Cooder, Emil Richards, Pharoah Sanders, Zakir Hussain, Greg Kurstin, Mileece, Shannon Terry and Imogen Heap. It also appears in television and film scores; the source mentions the American television series "Breaking Bad" and "True Blood" and the Danish film "In a Better World". The hollow body can be listened to as an acoustic instrument, while the solid body is better suited to amplified live work, since it is less prone to feedback.
陣列姆比拉琴起源於美國，由 Bill Wesley 發明，並與 Patrick: The array mbira originated in the United States, invented by Bill Wesley and made with Patrick Hadley in San Diego, California, with development beginning in the 1960s. It is a lamellophone redesigned on the basis of the mbira of Zimbabwe and Zambia, and it is an idiophone. Its important change is to arrange the pitches in a circle of fifths, so that the octaves of the same note are gathered together, which makes transposition and chords easier. It was later taken up by many musicians and entered television and film scores.
音色帶有豎琴或鐘聲般的清亮感。金屬舌片以輕壓後釋放發聲，指甲接觸可使音頭清晰，低: The timbre has the clear ring of a harp or a bell. The metal tines sound when pressed lightly and released, and the nail touching them makes the attack clear; the bass is flicked upwards with the pad of the thumb. Because the tines are bent, they produce more concordant overtones, especially at two octaves and a fifth, and are more concordant than other mbiras and kalimbas. The standard design has two and a half diatonic octaves arranged in a continuous circle of fifths; five octaves is common and some have seven; the octaves of the same note are grouped so that one finger can sound them together, and the volume is controlled by how the tine is pressed and released.
